app.title: Bird transect survey map with linked table
app.summary: The person loads a file of point observations from repeated walks along fixed survey lines and sees them as circles on an outline map of the study area, sized by count and coloured by habitat, beside a table of the records. They narrow what is shown by date range or a whole season, by habitat and by species, and a bar chart of totals per species and a header count follow every filter. Picking a row marks its point on the map, clicking a point scrolls to its row, and clicking a bar narrows everything to that species. They get a filtered view of where and when things were seen that they can step through season by season.

task.text: See where and when observations from repeated survey walks were made, and how the totals per category change between seasons and habitats.

data.text: Point observations from repeated walks along fixed survey lines, each with a date, the line, an observer, a category, a count, a habitat class and x/y coordinates in a local grid, drawn over a hard-coded outline of the study area and its survey lines.
data.item: one observation record: a count of one category at a point on a survey line on a date

stage.text: exploring survey data season by season

mechanism.text: A filter sidebar of date sliders, season buttons and habitat and species checklists drives a map of sized, coloured points, a bar chart of totals per category and a table of records, all redrawn together; selecting a row highlights its point, clicking a point scrolls to its row, and clicking a bar filters to that category.

field.text: avian ecology, wetland bird communities surveyed on transects

workflow.name: explore point records on a map, narrowed by time and category

steps.here: A CSV picked in the page replaces the generated records; it must have date, transect, observer, species, count, habitat, x and y columns, YYYY-MM-DD dates and numeric count and coordinates, and the page names the missing column or bad row instead of drawing an empty map.

steps.step: look over every item at a glance
steps.here: Every record is a translucent circle on the reserve outline with its transect lines, sized by count and coloured by habitat, with a size key, scale bar and north mark, beside a table of the records by date and transect.

steps.step: filter to the items that matter
steps.here: Checklists of habitats and species, each with its record count and All and None for species, narrow the map, chart and table together; the header and the table heading say how many records are showing out of the whole set.

steps.step: narrow to one time period and move between periods
steps.here: Two sliders set the from and to dates over the span of the data, and buttons jump straight to spring, summer, autumn or the whole period, so the same lines can be looked at season by season.

steps.step: total the shown items by category
steps.here: A bar chart totals the birds counted per species for whatever is filtered, largest first; clicking a bar narrows every view to that species and a button brings the rest back.

steps.step: find one item in both the map and the list
steps.here: Choosing a table row outlines its point and draws it on top; clicking a point highlights its row and scrolls the table to it; hovering a point shows its species, count, date, transect, habitat and observer.

distinctive: Records lie along fixed survey lines walked repeatedly, so the map draws the study-area outline, the lines, a scale bar and a north mark in a local metre grid instead of a basemap; a loaded file replaces the records but not the outline.
Circle size grows with the count, and the circles are translucent with small counts drawn over large groups, so a big flock does not hide the records under it.
Season buttons set the date range to a whole season in one click, for comparing the same lines across seasons.
Clicking a bar in the totals chart filters every view to that one category.
A loaded file is checked for its columns, date format and numbers, and the page names what is wrong rather than showing a blank map.
